stories.headline: 7.7 magnitude earthquake strikes off Indonesia's coast; buildings toppled, at least 2 killed
stories.title: 7.7 magnitude earthquake strikes off Indonesia's coast; buildings toppled, at least 2 killed
stories.summary: Indonesia, Aug 15: A 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early Saturday, collapsing buildings and homes, killing at least two people and causing panic in a region prone to deadly quakes. Authorities issued a tsunami warning but later lifted it when Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency said monitoring showed no significant sea-level changes that would pose a threat to coastal communities. The US Geological Survey said the quake hit Indonesia's Flores region with a depth of 10 km at 5:58 am local time. Its epicentre was 68 km north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. The initial quake was followed by several aftershocks. Preliminary reports from the Maumere Search and Rescue Agency said that at least two residents were killed and two others injured as the earthquake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, according to Indonesia's disaster management agency. Footage on local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution following the quake. Hospital staff moved equipment outdoors, including beds, IV stands and oxygen cylinders, and set up temporary treatment areas to adapt to emergency conditions. Quake felt on Flores island The quake was felt across much of Flores island with initial reports indicating heavy damage. Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground. "Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," she said. Students at St Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said the Rev Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores. "Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Tanga said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake." Indonesian authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks, and residents on the coastline to move to higher ground. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores island.

stories.headline: Four dead, five Army personnel missing after landslide, flash flood in Arunachal Pradesh
stories.title: Four dead, five Army personnel missing after landslide, flash flood in Arunachal Pradesh
stories.summary: Itanagar, Aug 15: Five Army personnel went missing after a flash flood triggered by heavy rainfall washed away two shelters in Arunachal Pradesh's Dibang Valley district, while four people died in a major landslide on a road construction site in Upper Subansiri district, officials said on Saturday. According to the State Emergency Operations Centre here, both incidents occurred on Friday evening. The landslide occurred at the Keojaring-Byaching road cutting site in Upper Subansiri district. While several people were buried under the debris, four people -- Tadu Baki, Taji Rai, Markosh Basumatari and Babul Ali -- were reported dead in the incident. The body of Babul Ali has been recovered, said the district disaster management officer of Upper Subansiri. Personnel from Nacho Police Station have been deployed for the search and recovery operation. Fire and Emergency Services personnel are also being mobilised from Daporijo, while a team of the State Disaster Response Force will assist in the operation. In Dibang Valley district, two shelters of the 5th Grenadier at the Pasu Pani Army Camp were washed away by a flash flood triggered by heavy rainfall on Friday evening. Officials said that the flash flood swept away seven Army personnel and two of them were rescued, while five remain missing. The missing personnel have been identified as Havaldar Upendar and Army personnel Kundan, Vinod, Aditya and Samunda. Two search and rescue teams from the 5th Grenadier have already been deployed. Teams comprising personnel of the 58th Battalion of the ITBP, 62 RCC of the General Reserve Engineer Force, local volunteers and the Arunachal Pradesh Police have been rushed to the site for the search operation. An SDRF team from Pasighat is also proceeding to Anini to assist in the rescue operation.

stories.title: NEADS and LIC HFL launch RAHAT project to aid 1,300 flood-hit families in Upper Assam

article_sentences: JORHAT: North-East Affected Area Development Society (NEADS), a local humanitarian organisation, in partnership with LIC Housing Finance Limited (LIC HFL), has launched emergency relief assistance for 1,300 flood-affected households across Charaideo and Sivasagar districts of Upper Assam under the LIC HFL RAHAT project.

The relief distribution was initiated in response to the continuing impact of floods across the two districts, which have disrupted household living conditions, food security, hygiene, and access to essential resources.
The RAHAT Project aims to provide timely and dignified humanitarian assistance to vulnerable families facing the immediate consequences of the floods.

The first-day distribution programme was held at Choladhara, Charaideo, in the presence of Abhinav Das, CSR Regional Lead (Northeast Zone), LIC Housing Finance Limited, along with the Chairperson of NEADS, members of the NEADS team, and the NEADS Emergency Response Team.

stories.headline: Torrential rains, cloudbursts, hailstorms lash Kashmir, trigger flash floods
stories.title: Torrential rains, cloudbursts, hailstorms lash Kashmir, trigger flash floods
stories.summary: Torrential rains and cloudbursts lashed parts of Kashmir on Friday, triggering flash floods in south Kashmir and damaging roads, paddy fields and apple orchards, while the Meteorological Centre Srinagar forecast isolated thunderstorms and gusty winds over the next few days. Plains of Kashmir received rain, while several upper areas of south Kashmir witnessed hailstorms and cloudbursts, with swollen streams and sudden surges in water reported from vulnerable areas. Officials from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Srinagar, said parts of Srinagar and the south Kashmir districts of Anantnag, Pulwama, Shopian and Kulgam were lashed by rain and hailstorms. In Anantnag district, intense localized showers in the Pahalgam area triggered flash floods on Friday evening, damaging a temporary road at Awoora, and disrupting traffic again on the Bijbehara-Langanbal-Pahalgam route. The sudden surge in water swept away portions of the makeshift road, forcing authorities to suspend vehicular movement along the stretch. Commuters were advised to avoid the route until restoration work is completed. A cloudburst was reported from Chaki Ishardas-Wantrag in the Shangus area of Anantnag, triggering flash floods in the locality. Residents said a sudden gush of water inundated streets and farmland, with water entering residential areas and damaging sprawling paddy and apple fields. They said the flash floods also damaged a portion of the road, bringing traffic to a halt. In Shopian district, an intense hailstorm struck around 3 p.m., sweeping through Feripora, Mandujan, Adijan, Kapran and several adjoining villages. Hailstorm also hit, in the Nihama area of nearby Kulgam district. Farmers said marble-sized hailstones battered apple orchards for nearly 10 to 15 minutes, leaving apples bruised and damaged. “The hailstones completely damaged the orchards. In just a few minutes, our labour went down the drain,” said Farooq Ahmad, a farmer from Mandujan. He said the hailstorm struck at a critical time, with harvesting of the Kullu variety of apples only weeks away. “We had been waiting for the harvest, but the damage has put everything at risk,” he said. Farmers said the extent of the losses would become clearer over the coming days as damaged fruit begins to fall and the impact on marketable produce is assessed. The latest hailstorm comes just days after a powerful windstorm on August 6 caused extensive damage to apple orchards across more than 26 villages in Shopian. Farmers had reported widespread fruit drop and damage to trees following the storm. The successive weather events have added to concerns among growers in one of Kashmir’s major apple-producing districts, where a large section of the population depends on horticulture for its livelihood. In Pulwama district, water levels in streams in the Watal Nagabal area of Tral also rose following the rains, prompting concern among residents living close to water channels. Gusty winds were also reported near the railway station in Pampore and several other areas in South Kashmir. A chinar -tree was uprooted in Salia area of Anantnag amid strong winds. However, no loss of life or property was reported. The Meteorological Centre Srinagar has forecast isolated thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of 30-40 kmph across Kashmir over the next seven days, from August 15 to 20. The weather department has warned of possible landslides, mudslides, flash floods and shooting stones at vulnerable locations during this period. It has advised people to remain cautious during rainfall, particularly in areas prone to landslides, flash floods and other weather-related disruptions. Authorities have also urged residents and commuters in vulnerable areas to remain alert and avoid unnecessary travel during intense spells of rain.

stories.headline: J&K youth must ensure mistakes of past are never repeated: LG Sinha
stories.title: J&K youth must ensure mistakes of past are never repeated: LG Sinha
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 14: The Lieutenant Governor, Manoj Sinha, today attended the solemn observance of ‘Partition Horrors Remembrance Day’ at Tagore Hall, Srinagar. The event was marked by collective remembrance and a reaffirmation of national unity. In his address on the occasion, the Lieutenant Governor paid heartfelt tribute to all those citizens who endured unimaginable suffering during the partition of 1947 and whose sacrifices continue to inspire generations. The Lieutenant Governor emphasised that the wound of partition continues to exist as a pain in the collective consciousness of every Indian. “Decades after the partition, their sacrifice reminds us that the wound remains unhealed, lingering as a generational pain in India’s collective soul. On Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, we are not merely recalling the past but we are giving voice to those millions whose voices were taken away from them. I wish to reiterate with firm resolve that we will not allow their pain to be buried in the dust of history. Remembering them is fulfilling our duty towards humanity. We will preserve their memories. Remembering them with complete truthfulness, honesty, and utmost sensitivity is the most sacred tribute. I believe that their stories are an indelible chapter of our national consciousness, and their sacrifice will forever remain alive in the soul of Mother India,” the Lieutenant Governor said. The Lieutenant Governor urged the people of UT of Jammu and Kashmir to treat this day as an occasion of introspection and national resolve. He called upon the youth, farmers, workers, and women to rise with courage and determination, to turn the pace of time towards progress and harmony. The Lieutenant Governor praised the resilience of people who rebuilt their lives with courage and enriched the country’s social fabric and cultural heritage with historic traditions and values. ‘Today’s occasion is an opportunity to acknowledge the pain of the past and strengthen our unwavering commitment to peace, harmony and national unity. This day reminds us that only the lessons of history can make the future secure and humane,” the Lieutenant Governor said. He noted that the partition divided families and displaced communities from Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir and Chhamb. He paid tribute to those who faced decades-long discrimination within the UT due to Article 370. The Lieutenant Governor said that Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi ended their suffering and granted them equal rights like any other citizen of the country. The Lieutenant Governor also paid tribute the countless families who sacrificed during the tribal invasion months after partition. “Within a few months of partition, enemies of the nation carried out terror attack under the cover of tribal invasions. Indian army and people fought bravely. The struggle and sacrifice of countless families are an integral part of the collective memory of Jammu and Kashmir. Today, I humbly pay tribute to the patience, hard work, and unbroken patriotism of all those families,” he said. Addressing the youth, the Lieutenant Governor emphasised that partition is not merely history but a living memory of millions of families. He urged them to learn from the experiences of the past, to reject enmity and communal bitterness, and to build bridges of trust. He called upon them to construct a developed India that is inclusive and empowered. “The youth of Jammu Kashmir must ensure that the mistakes of the past are never repeated in the future. Where walls were once raised, you must build bridges of trust and construct a Viksit Bharat that is inclusive,” the Lieutenant Governor said. The Lieutenant Governor reminded the gathering that India’s strength lies in its diversity. From Kashmir to Kanyakumari, from Gujarat to Goa, from Assam to Arunachal Pradesh, India is a confluence of languages, cultures, traditions, and beliefs, he said. “Through partition, enemies of the nation tried to destroy this spirit of unity in diversity, but India has continuously moved forward with pride and confidence. We must take a pledge to acquaint future generations with the pain of partition, to strengthen peace and harmony, and to ensure that such a tragedy is never repeated. Building a self-reliant Jammu Kashmir is a shared duty and national unity remains the bedrock of our strength, security and collective progress,” the Lieutenant Governor said. The Lieutenant Governor visited the photo exhibition on Partition Horrors Remembrance Day. A Two- minute silence was observed in memory of those who lost their lives during the Partition of India.

stories.headline: J&K paid price for Indus Waters Treaty, it must remain suspended: Omar Abdullah
stories.title: J&K paid price for Indus Waters Treaty, it must remain suspended: Omar Abdullah
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 14: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday hit out at Pakistan for staking a claim over the waters of rivers flowing through Jammu and Kashmir, questioning Islamabad’s professed sympathy for Kashmiris while opposing the region’s use of its own water resources. Abdullah was responding to questions from reporters regarding Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s latest remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), in which he described water as Pakistan’s “red line” and warned of a “direct response” if the country’s water supplies were threatened. “We have always been saying that our blood has been sucked — these are our rivers. We had the first right on this. Pakistanis say they are great sympathisers of Kashmiris. But when it comes to water, their sympathy disappears. Where was their sympathy when we were denied permission to use our rivers?” Abdullah said. The Chief Minister said the distribution of the Indus river system under the treaty had left Jammu and Kashmir bearing the consequences, arguing that India retained the waters of the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej while the Chenab, Jhelum and Indus were allocated to Pakistan. “From then until today, we are suffering the consequences of this Indus Waters Treaty,” Abdullah said, adding that the restrictions had affected the region’s ability to fully utilise its water resources. stories.headline: Modi warns of weaponisation of resources, sea routes; urges energy self-reliance
stories.title: Modi warns of weaponisation of resources, sea routes; urges energy self-reliance
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 15: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday warned that the weaponisation of resources and strategic sea routes by some countries posed risks to India's economic security, calling for greater self-reliance in energy to reduce the country's vulnerability to overseas supplies. Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort on India's 80th Independence Day, Modi said India needed to strengthen domestic capacity in critical areas, including energy and minerals, as geopolitical tensions increasingly exposed the risks of dependence on external sources. Without naming any country, Modi said resources ranging from fuel and medicines to technology were increasingly being used as instruments of geopolitical pressure, while strategic geographical routes were also being weaponised. His remarks come against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war with Iran and Tehran's retaliation, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for global energy supplies. The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman handled about 20 million barrels per day of oil and petroleum products in 2025, equivalent to roughly a quarter of global seaborne oil trade, according to the International Energy Agency. It also carried almost 20 per cent of global LNG trade, leaving major Asian importers particularly exposed to any prolonged disruption. The conflict has sharply reduced maritime traffic through the strait and pushed up energy and shipping costs. Renewed tanker attacks have stalled efforts to resolve the conflict. For India, the disruption has highlighted the risks posed by its dependence on imported energy. The country has had to seek alternative LNG supplies from countries including Oman, the United States, Nigeria and Angola after uncertainty over Gulf shipments, while Indian refiners have also moved to diversify crude purchases. India has already broadened its energy sourcing, importing crude from 41 countries and LNG from 15, up from 27 and six respectively, as New Delhi seeks to insulate the economy from geopolitical shocks. The Strait of Hormuz is particularly important to India because much of the energy passing through it is bound for Asia. The IEA estimates that India received nearly half of its crude oil that transited the strait in 2025. It also obtained almost two-thirds of its LNG supplies through the waterway. Modi said the geopolitical conflicts have underscored the importance of becoming self-reliant in energy. India, which imports nearly 90 per cent of its crude oil requirements and about half of its natural gas needs, is seeking to tap its largely underexplored offshore reserves as part of a broader push to strengthen energy security, he said, citing the recently approved the Rs 84,084-crore Samudra Manthan National Offshore Exploration Scheme, aimed at accelerating exploration for oil and gas in deepwater and ultra-deepwater areas over the next five years. The programme will support seismic surveys, exploratory drilling and shared offshore infrastructure, with the government seeking to attract greater investment and technology into India's offshore basins. He said the government has also opened up 99 per cent of India's sedimentary basins for oil and gas exploration and production, expanding access to areas that were previously largely off-limits to commercial exploration. The move is intended to unlock domestic hydrocarbon resources and reduce India's exposure to global energy-price and supply shocks. The Prime Minister went on to list achievements of his government in the last 12 years - expansion of piped cooking gas coverage from 70 cities to 700 cities, with the fuel - an alternate to LPG which is largely imported from the Middle East - now being supplied to 1.75 crore households as against 22 lakh in 2014. Also, generation of electricity from the sun's solar energy has jumped to 160 gigawatt from 2 GW a decade back, he said. Energy security has emerged as a central element of Modi's broader push for an "Atmanirbhar Bharat", or self-reliant India. The government has also sought to expand domestic exploration of critical minerals and increase the role of nuclear power and other non-fossil energy sources. In 2024-25, crude oil imports were valued at about USD 137 billion, while petroleum products and LNG imports were worth USD 24 billion and USD 15 billion respectively.

stories.headline: The World Carries India Within It
stories.title: The World Carries India Within It
stories.summary: On 15 August 2026, India will raise its flag for the eightieth time. Seventy-nine years since the British left. Seventy-nine years since freedom arrived carrying both a promise and a question: What would we do with it? Every Independence Day, we remember the struggle, the marches, the prisons, the salt, the sacrifice, the long and wounded birth of a nation. But perhaps Independence Day is also a time to remember another inheritance, the ideas, inventions, practices and traditions that India has sent out into the world. Not as a boast, not as a claim staked on history, but as a quiet reckoning with the ways in which knowledge travels, leaving one civilization, entering another, and finally becoming so ordinary that nobody remembers where it began. One of India’s most influential contributions came from mathematics. Its story was not the work of one mathematician alone. In the fifth century, Aryabhata developed a place-value system that depended on the idea of an empty position, creating what we might call a silent zero. Although he did not use a separate written symbol for zero, his system required a placeholder to distinguish numerical values according to their position. More than a century later, Brahmagupta gave that silence a mathematical identity. In the seventh century, he described zero, or Shunya, as a number in its own right and established rules for calculating with it. Together with the decimal and place-value systems, their work transformed calculation and gave the world a numerical language in which stars could be measured, economies could be built and machines could think. The mobile phone in your hand, the satellite circling above you and the spreadsheet waiting for its next figure all carry, somewhere inside their intricate machinery, the inheritance of that ancient Indian insight. But India’s mathematical imagination did not end with zero. Indian scholars made significant advances in algebra, geometry, astronomy, trigonometry and the calculation of pi. Aryabhata wrote about the rotation of the Earth and developed methods for calculating astronomical positions. The Sulba Sutras contained early geometrical knowledge, while later mathematicians such as Bhaskara II explored ideas that anticipated aspects of algebra and calculus. These achievements remind us that mathematics is not merely a collection of formulas. It is a way of asking the universe to reveal its pattern. Chess travelled in a different way. It began, historians broadly believe, in the form of Chaturanga, a game of war and strategy played in India during the Gupta period. Its pieces represented the forces of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. Over centuries, the game moved through Persia and the Arab world before reaching Europe, changing shape as it travelled. Today, a chessboard can be found in a schoolroom in Srinagar, a café in Paris, a park in Moscow or a championship hall in Chennai. India’s gift was not only the game. It was the idea that conflict could be studied, contained and transformed into thought. India’s contributions to language were equally profound. Panini’s Ashtadhyayi, composed more than two thousand years ago, presented Sanskrit grammar through an extraordinarily precise system of rules. Its structure has drawn the attention of modern linguists and computer scientists because of its formal, almost algorithmic quality. It showed that language could be observed not only as poetry and expression, but also as a system with patterns, structures and transformations. In India, language was not simply a tool for communication. It was a universe to be examined. The country’s reputation as a centre of learning is older than its modern universities. Takshashila and Nalanda were places where students and scholars gathered from different regions to study medicine, astronomy, philosophy, grammar and logic. Nalanda, in present-day Bihar, drew scholars from China and Central Asia. It belonged to an age when knowledge did not always arrive divided into departments, syllabi and examination halls. It moved more freely, like water finding its level. India’s medical traditions also travelled through time and across borders. Ayurveda developed a holistic approach to health, placing attention on diet, herbs, daily routines and the relationship between body and mind. The Charaka Samhita explored internal medicine, while the surgical writings attributed to Sushruta described procedures and instruments that reveal the sophistication of early Indian surgery. These traditions have immense historical significance. Their modern use, however, must be approached responsibly. Ancient systems may inform contemporary wellness, but they cannot replace evidence-based clinical care. India also made remarkable advances in metallurgy. The Iron Pillar of Delhi, known for its resistance to corrosion, remains a striking example of ancient Indian metalworking. Indian wootz steel, produced through a sophisticated crucible process, became renowned for its quality and influenced the development of famous Damascus blades. Behind these achievements lay an understanding of heat, carbon, minerals and materials that was practical, experimental and highly refined. Few Indian traditions have travelled as visibly as yoga. Once practised by relatively small circles of seekers, yoga now appears in schools, studios, hospitals, gyms and living rooms across the world. It has been stretched, commercialised, branded and sometimes separated from its philosophical roots. Yet beneath the mats, the postures and the breath-counting remains an old proposition: that the body is not merely a machine carrying the mind, but a doorway into it. The United Nations recognised 21 June as the International Day of Yoga in 2014, and UNESCO placed yoga on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016. Long before institutions gave it official recognition, people had already discovered what the practice could offer: a pause in a world that profits from permanent motion. India’s philosophical gifts have travelled even further. Buddhism carried ideas of compassion, mindfulness and freedom from suffering across Asia and eventually into the wider world. Jainism placed non-violence and respect for all living beings at the centre of spiritual life. Sikhism brought together equality, courage, devotion and service. And then there was ahimsa, non-violence, not as weakness and not as surrender, but as a force capable of unsettling an empire. Mahatma Gandhi transformed it into a method of mass resistance. Martin Luther King Jr. studied and adapted its principles during the American civil rights movement. Others, in different countries and different struggles, found in it a way to confront power without becoming its mirror. India’s gifts have not travelled only through books and laboratories. They have travelled in song, spice, fabric, rhythm and story. Indian cotton and textiles were traded across the ancient world. Hindustani and Carnatic music carry centuries of listening. Bharatanatyam and Kathak turn the body into language. Indian food crosses borders in tiffin boxes, restaurants, kitchens and family recipes altered by migration. Indian cinema, made in many languages and many emotional registers, has created its own geography of longing. Its songs travel farther than its plots. Its faces become familiar in places where the languages are not. The world may not understand every word, but it recognises the gesture: the mother waiting, the lover returning, the family breaking and remaking itself. These are not small things. A culture survives not only in monuments, but in what people hum while washing dishes, in what they cook when they are homesick and in the stories they tell their children before sleep. Modern India has continued to send its ideas outward. The Indian Space Research Organisation has shown that ambitious scientific work need not always be accompanied by extravagant spending. The Mars Orbiter Mission, launched in 2013, entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 on its first attempt. ISRO describes it as India’s first interplanetary mission and notes that its success demonstrated the country’s ability to carry out a complex mission in a cost-effective manner. But science is not a miracle performed by a nation. It is the result of people: scientists, technicians, teachers, programmers, machinists, students and workers whose names rarely appear in celebration speeches. The same is true of the Universal Serial Bus, now so familiar that its name has almost disappeared into everyday language. Indian-American computer architect Ajay V. Bhatt led the team at Intel that developed the technology. The device that connects our phones, cameras, hard drives and laptops is another reminder that innovation often arrives quietly, then becomes indispensable. India’s scientific contribution also includes the work of Jagadish Chandra Bose in radio and plant science, the development of fibre-optic communication by Narinder Singh Kapany and the achievements of Indian doctors, engineers, researchers and entrepreneurs working across the world. The story of India’s gifts is therefore not a straight line from an ancient past to a glorious present. It is a river with many streams. Some flow from Sanskrit texts and temple schools. Some come from laboratories, universities and space centres. Some emerge from workshops, kitchens, farms, weaving communities and ordinary homes. There is a danger, however, in making a catalogue of India’s achievements. A country can become so enchanted by its ancient glory that it forgets the living people standing in its shadow. What does it mean to praise Nalanda while schools crumble? To celebrate Ayurveda while public hospitals struggle? To speak of the wisdom of non-violence while hatred is made profitable? To celebrate the sophistication of Indian mathematics while children are denied the education needed to understand it? To claim the generosity of Indian civilization while dissenters are silenced, minorities are frightened and the poor are asked to be grateful for survival? The question is not whether India has given the world great things. It has. The more difficult question is whether India is still willing to give the world what its oldest traditions demanded of it: curiosity without arrogance, knowledge without ownership, strength without cruelty, faith without hatred and progress without the destruction of the vulnerable. Zero teaches us that absence can contain possibility. Astronomy teaches us to look beyond the limits of the earth. Chess teaches us that every move alters the board. Yoga teaches us to breathe before we act. Language teaches us that every word carries a history. Metallurgy teaches us that patient knowledge can outlast its makers. Music teaches us that memory can be carried in sound. Ahimsa teaches us that power need not resemble violence. Perhaps these are not merely India’s gifts to the world. Perhaps they are instructions sent back to India from its own past. So, when the flag rises on 15 August, let it not be only a symbol of what India once overcame, or a banner beneath which we recite what India once achieved. Let it be a question moving through the country, from the ramparts of the Red Fort in Delhi to the paddy fields of Punjab, the apple orchards of Kashmir and the fishing villages of Kerala; from the farmers who read the sky, to the weavers who preserve memory in thread, to the students building robots in Atal Tinkering Labs, to the scientists sending India’s imagination beyond the earth: What will we do with what we have inherited? Because a nation is not made great by the treasures it locks inside its history. It is made great by what it protects in the present, by what it imagines for the future, and by whether, after giving the world zero, India can still find a way to make sure that no one, no child, no community, no language and no memory is treated as if they count for nothing. (The author is a columnist)

A culture survives not only in monuments, but in what people hum while washing dishes, in what they cook when they are homesick and in the stories they tell their children before sleep.
Modern India has continued to send its ideas outward.
The Indian Space Research Organisation has shown that ambitious scientific work need not always be accompanied by extravagant spending.
The Mars Orbiter Mission, launched in 2013, entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 on its first attempt.
ISRO describes it as India’s first interplanetary mission and notes that its success demonstrated the country’s ability to carry out a complex mission in a cost-effective manner.
But science is not a miracle performed by a nation.
It is the result of people: scientists, technicians, teachers, programmers, machinists, students and workers whose names rarely appear in celebration speeches.
The same is true of the Universal Serial Bus, now so familiar that its name has almost disappeared into everyday language.
Indian-American computer architect Ajay V. Bhatt led the team at Intel that developed the technology.
The device that connects our phones, cameras, hard drives and laptops is another reminder that innovation often arrives quietly, then becomes indispensable.

India’s scientific contribution also includes the work of Jagadish Chandra Bose in radio and plant science, the development of fibre-optic communication by Narinder Singh Kapany and the achievements of Indian doctors, engineers, researchers and entrepreneurs working across the world.
The story of India’s gifts is therefore not a straight line from an ancient past to a glorious present.
It is a river with many streams.
Some flow from Sanskrit texts and temple schools.
Some come from laboratories, universities and space centres.
Some emerge from workshops, kitchens, farms, weaving communities and ordinary homes.
There is a danger, however, in making a catalogue of India’s achievements.
A country can become so enchanted by its ancient glory that it forgets the living people standing in its shadow.
What does it mean to praise Nalanda while schools crumble?
To celebrate Ayurveda while public hospitals struggle?
To speak of the wisdom of non-violence while hatred is made profitable?
To celebrate the sophistication of Indian mathematics while children are denied the education needed to understand it?
To claim the generosity of Indian civilization while dissenters are silenced, minorities are frightened and the poor are asked to be grateful for survival?
The question is not whether India has given the world great things.
It has.

The more difficult question is whether India is still willing to give the world what its oldest traditions demanded of it: curiosity without arrogance, knowledge without ownership, strength without cruelty, faith without hatred and progress without the destruction of the vulnerable.
Zero teaches us that absence can contain possibility.
Astronomy teaches us to look beyond the limits of the earth.
Chess teaches us that every move alters the board.
Yoga teaches us to breathe before we act.
Language teaches us that every word carries a history.
Metallurgy teaches us that patient knowledge can outlast its makers.
Music teaches us that memory can be carried in sound.
Ahimsa teaches us that power need not resemble violence.
Perhaps these are not merely India’s gifts to the world.
Perhaps they are instructions sent back to India from its own past.
So, when the flag rises on 15 August, let it not be only a symbol of what India once overcame, or a banner beneath which we recite what India once achieved.

Let it be a question moving through the country, from the ramparts of the Red Fort in Delhi to the paddy fields of Punjab, the apple orchards of Kashmir and the fishing villages of Kerala; from the farmers who read the sky, to the weavers who preserve memory in thread, to the students building robots in Atal Tinkering Labs, to the scientists sending India’s imagination beyond the earth: What will we do with what we have inherited?
Because a nation is not made great by the treasures it locks inside its history.

It is made great by what it protects in the present, by what it imagines for the future, and by whether, after giving the world zero, India can still find a way to make sure that no one, no child, no community, no language and no memory is treated as if they count for nothing.
(The author is a columnist).

stories.title: India at 80
stories.summary: On 15 August 2026, India will mark its 80th Independence Day. The occasion should not be limited to remembering the end of British rule. It should also make us ask a basic question: what does freedom mean in the actual lives of Indian citizens? India became politically independent in 1947, and the Constitution came into force in 1950. Its Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. These principles are not ceremonial words. They are the standards by which the Republic should judge its own progress. India’s democratic achievement is significant. It adopted universal adult franchise from the beginning of the Republic and has maintained regular elections despite deep differences of religion, language, caste, region and economic condition. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, voter turnout was 66.10 per cent. Women constituted 48.62 per cent of registered electors, and their turnout was 65.78 per cent, compared with 65.55 per cent for men. These figures show strong participation. But democracy is more than voting. It also requires equal rights, accountable institutions and the freedom to question those who exercise public power. The Constitution provides the foundation for these rights. Article 14 guarantees equality before law. Article 15 prohibits discrimination on specified grounds, including religion, race, caste and sex. Article 19 protects important freedoms, including speech and expression. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. These provisions establish a clear principle: the State must respect the rights and dignity of every citizen. Yet legal equality does not automatically create social equality. B.R. Ambedkar examined this problem in Annihilation of Caste. He argued that political democracy cannot survive when social relations deny equality. In The Buddha and His Dhamma, he placed liberty, equality and fraternity at the centre of social life. The Constitution itself recognises the problem of inequality. Article 38 directs the State to reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities. Article 39 calls for adequate means of livelihood and seeks to prevent excessive concentration of wealth. India has made major economic progress. The World Bank reports that since 2000 India’s economy has nearly quadrupled in real terms, while real per-capita income has almost tripled. The IMF projects 7.0 per cent real GDP growth in 2026. These achievements matter. But GDP growth is not the same as human development. Growth becomes meaningful when it creates secure work, raises incomes and improves education, healthcare and living conditions. India has also reduced poverty. But poverty cannot be understood only through an income threshold. A family may move above a poverty line and still face poor housing, inadequate healthcare, weak education or insecure employment. Employment is therefore a central test of economic freedom. The PLFS 2025 recorded labour-force participation of 59.3 per cent among people aged 15 years and above. The rate was 79.1 per cent for men and only 40.0 per cent for women. This gap is a serious equality issue. Women need equal access to paid work and public decision-making. Constitutional equality must be visible in people’s actual opportunities, not only in legal provisions. Gandhi’s Hind Swaraj gives freedom a wider meaning. For Gandhi, swaraj was not simply the replacement of British rulers by Indian rulers. It also required self-rule, personal responsibility, social cooperation and moral discipline. Political independence was therefore the beginning of freedom, not its completion. Education is equally important. Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen, while Article 51A(h) asks citizens to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. Education should enable citizens to examine evidence, question false claims and disagree peacefully. Without these abilities, the right to vote cannot by itself create a strong democracy. Rabindranath Tagore’s Nationalism offers another important warning. Tagore opposed nationalism when political power was placed above human dignity. His vision of a society “where the mind is without fear” remains relevant. Legal freedom is incomplete when people live under fear caused by poverty, discrimination, violence or arbitrary power. Human development provides another measure of progress. The UNDP Human Development Report 2025 ranked India 130th among 193 countries, with an HDI of 0.685 for 2023. The report estimates that inequality reduces India’s HDI by 30.7 per cent. The lesson is direct: national income matters, but health, education and living standards matter equally. Fraternity is another essential part of freedom. Article 51A(e) asks citizens to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood. India contains many religions, languages, castes and regional identities. These differences do not threaten national unity when all citizens receive equal constitutional protection. National unity should be based on equal citizenship, not social uniformity. Environmental protection is also connected with human freedom. Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment, while Article 51A(g) places an environmental duty on citizens. Clean air, safe water and a healthy environment are basic conditions of a dignified life. India now looks towards 2047, the centenary of Independence. The goal should be precise. Development should provide equal educational opportunities, dignified employment, accessible healthcare, greater participation of women, accountable institutions and equal protection of law. Ambedkar taught that political equality requires social equality. Gandhi connected freedom with swaraj and responsibility. Tagore connected freedom with reason and freedom from fear. Their ideas remain relevant because political independence alone cannot guarantee human freedom. At 80, India should celebrate what it has achieved, but it should also confront what remains unfinished. Independence freed India from colonial rule. The Constitution demands freedom, equality and dignity for its people. The real test is whether that promise is lived by every citizen. Dr. Sabzar Ahmad Bhat, PhD, Central University of Gujarat.

stories.headline: Borders Defines Indian: But Who Defines Border Citizen?
stories.title: Borders Defines Indian: But Who Defines Border Citizen?
stories.summary: As the 80 th anniversary of Independence Day dawns, the country will simply go into an overdrive with customary grandeur. The Tricolour will flutter atop important buildings; schoolchildren will sing patriotic songs, and speeches will extol the sacrifices that won us freedom from our colonial masters. A nation- state is defined by two of its very distinct facets—its people who populate its entire length and breadth and off course the national boundaries/borders. Both of these entities find ample space and discourse in its constitution and are complementary to each other. Not one of them individually can define the concept of a nation-state on its own steam. No wonder eighty years back, when Cyril Radcliffe the British lawyer cum boundary commission chairman set out his task of defining the national boundaries of India and Pakistan in a mere forty five days span , even he wouldn’t have realized the importance of carving out such a ‘cartographic lineation’. Since this lineation was followed by one of the biggest human displacements with bloody repercussions in modern times across the Radcliffe line, hence the uniqueness of this partition.The borders of a country are not merely ‘cartographic labyrinthine’ but a place where the republic is tested every single day. It is where the idea of India ceases to be an abstraction and becomes a lived reality. Ironically, while the border defines India’s geography, the ‘border citizen’ often remains invisible in India’s policymaking. For close to seventy nine years, India has viewed its national borders primarily through the prism of military strategy, investing in troops, weapons, surveillance and other infra to protect its territorial integrity. These investments are indispensible no doubt, but they also reveal a deeper flaw in our national thinking right from 1947. We have treated borders as military spaces to be defended rather than living spaces to be nurtured. This distinction matters, and hence my endeavour to pen down this write up on India’s 80 th Independence day to put under the scanner such a distinction which may not portend well for our country if left untreated. A nation-state is not merely secured by its armed forces guarding its borders. It is secured when citizens choose to live there with dignity, confidence and hope. Every inhabited village on the border is a declaration of national sovereignty. Every family that refuses to abandon its ancestral home despite enemy shelling, infiltration or isolation is performing an act of national service that rarely finds mention from the ramparts of Red fort of India. Nowhere is this reality more visible than in Jammu & Kashmir. Border residents have lived through wars since 1947, terrorist violence, repeated ceasefire violations and prolonged uncertainty. Children have grown up distinguishing mortar fire from festival fireworks, farmers have cultivated fields under the shadow of sniper fire and many more such vagaries as thrown up by our inimical western neighbour at us. These are not isolated tragedies. But represent a way of life that few Indians living hundreds of Kilometers away can fully comprehend. Out of a stated fifteen thousand kilometers of total land boundary of India touching seven neighbouring nations, how much of border is actually under fire of ours? I may dare say only that which abuts our western neighbour in the UT of J&K and now under an uneasy calm punctuated by repeated ceasefire violations. Isn’t it suitable time on the anvil of 80 th Independence Day of India, that these hapless people are not left to the mercy of geo-political machinations of this sub-continent which are played with utter disregard to their wellbeing? Be that as it may, yet public policy frequently views border districts through the lens of relief rather than resilience. Compensation is announced after damage, roads are sanctioned after strategic necessity arises. Same is the case with a plethora of welfare schemes involving schools, hospitals and employment opportunities. In the after math of mayhem unleashed by Pakistan last year during ‘Op Sindoor’ on our border villages abutting both the IB and the LC, stories of continued neglect, administrative cum bureaucratic apathy emanate from media circles regarding laggardly pace of redevelopment of damaged infra. Leave alone relief, resilience is a far cry for us to come on top of the things as they stand today. The contrast with China is instructive. Both India & China threw out the yolk of slavery in the late 1940s. With a gap of only two years in between i.e. 1947 and 1949 respectively, China has pursued an integrated border strategy in which civilian settlements, economic development and military preparedness reinforce each other thereby surpassing India both in thought and action. Many of the readers of my article may argue that being a totalitarian cum communist nation, for China the concept of a nation-state supersedes its denizens. This is passé, simple and straight. For the sake of argument even if I do take this concept as viable, then may I ask why India has woken up lately to emulate the same concept in the format of VVP (Vibrant village programme now? The villages of China all along the LAC in our context present themselves the ‘Chinese instrument of national security, signaling that the writ of mandarins of power in Beijing runs not only in their national capital but right till the last village of theirs. Though India as stated above has lately started in the right earnest to rectify decades of its inertia in such matters, by kicking starting programmes like the VVP it is too late and too less. The intent though commendable, the scheme doesn’t inspire that much confidence. As late as few weeks back the PM in one of his discourses with the youth of India under the aegis of DIYLD (Developed India young leader’s dialogue) presented an idea before them of visiting border villages, stay and connect with them instead of using the virtual media to do so. This suggestion by our honourable PM throws an interesting question instead—‘Is merely encouraging the youth of India to visit these border villages enough? Can these cosmetics change the dismal situation as found present in these frontier areas? I shall not dwell much upon this topic, since it is being tackled by me in a separate article from Rising Kashmir paper. Border citizens per se ought to be placed head and shoulders above the rest of populace of our country. Their defining attributes being derived from their very stay in the border areas and acting as the sentinels of a democratic dispensation in a region surrounded by theocratic countries. As India enters its eightieth year of independence, perhaps the time is ripe enough to redefine the citizenry of our border areas who away from the din of the mainstream living of India are silently carving out an existence for themselves based on true values of nationalism. The strength of a nation cannot be measured in terms of its military or economic might. But from the confidence of its citizens living at its farthest edge. If the border defines India’s territorial identity, then the ‘border citizens’ defines its moral identity. How India treats those who stand at its frontiers reveals what kind of republic it truly is. (The writer is a retired army officer and a regular scribe of Rising Kashmir. He can be approached on his email: slalotra4729@gmail.com)

Former Supreme Court judge Justice K.M. Joseph has suggested that a permanent and regular Constitution Bench may be constituted in the Top Court, as an institutional reform, to decide on important issues in the country.
Justice Joseph made the suggestion while speaking at event organised by the Kerala High Court Advocates' Association (KHCAA) and the Constitution Debate Club.

Justice Joseph delivered a lecture on the topic 'Liberty Across Continents: The Enduring Legacy of the American Declaration of Independence & the Constitution of India' in the event held to commemorate the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence.

The suggestion to have a permanent Constitutional Bench was made while pointing out the long pendency of important matters, including a reference made in 2016 on the question as to whether courts can dictate timelines to a Speaker when deciding anti-defection petitions.
Justice Joseph quoted a few examples in different States, where there was inordinate delay on the side of the Speaker in deciding these petitions.

It happened in Maharashtra, it happened earlier also.
It is happening right in front of our eyes.

stories.title: 'Should India Remain Underdeveloped?' : Supreme Court Slams Union's Opposition To Adopt Global Norms On Food Package Labelling

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: "The World should know that India is very much concerned about the overall health of its citizens, more particularly the growing children," the Court said.

The Supreme Court recently disapproved of the Union's stand that it can't follow international standards when it comes to issuing interpretative warnings of high sugar, sodium or fat content on packaged food items.
The Court questioned if India should remain underdeveloped, ignoring that obesity remains a significant public health concern.

The observations were made in the context of the failure of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to implement the Front-of-Package labelling (FOPL), a standard adopted at the international level.
It may be recalled that the Court on February 10 observed that FSSAI failed to file a satisfactory affidavit on mandatory compliance with FOPL.
It directed them to file another compliance report, and the matter was then taken up on August 13 before a bench comprising Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran.

However, the Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar(for FSSAI) informed the bench that it can't comply with the FOPL as Indian dietary standards are different from those followed internationally.
This didn't sit well with the Court, which disapproved of the Union's stand that India can't match the standards of developed countries.
The Court observed: "We do not approve the stance of the Union when it says that it is not possible to match with international standards, more particularly, developed countries.
That's the question we are putting forward for the Union to consider.
The World should know that India is very much concerned about the overall health of its citizens, more particularly the growing children."
It reiterated that the matter concerns the health of the citizens, more particularly growing children whose health can't be compromised.

stories.headline: India in U.S. crosshairs again — White House report cites countries ‘enabling’ China’s tariff evasions
stories.title: India in U.S. crosshairs again — White House report cites countries ‘enabling’ China’s tariff evasions
stories.summary: The report has identified more than 40 countries associated with “elevated illegal transshipment risk”; the U.S. has named the Pune-Gujarat-Chennai belt as one of the areas enabling China
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India is once again in the U.S.’ crosshairs, this time for allegedly allowing China to evade U.S. tariffs by routing its exports through the country.
The latest allegations are part of a new White House report called ‘The Great Transhipment Scam’.
In particular, the U.S. has named the Pune-Gujarat-Chennai belt as one of the areas “enabling” China to evade tariffs to the detriment of supply chains in the U.S.

This comes at a time when the U.S. has already imposed a 10% tariff on India for not doing enough to stop the import of goods made using forced labour, and is in the process of enacting legislation that would see tariffs of up to 100% imposed on India for its import of Russian oil.
An ongoing investigation by the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) related to excess capacity could see further tariffs on top of all this.
The U.S. had in 2018 levied tariffs ranging from 7.5% to 100% on goods from China under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 for unfair trade and tech practices.
On July 24, 2026, it added a further 12.5% tariff for forced-labour compliance gaps.
“After their imposition, Chinese exporters increasingly routed goods through third countries,” the White House report noted.

“Products that previously moved directly from China to the United States were shipped through jurisdictions where limited assembly, finishing, repackaging, relabeling, or documentation changes could create the appearance of a different national origin.”
The report has identified more than 40 countries associated with “elevated illegal transshipment risk”, with India among the top “enablers” of China’s evasion of tariffs.
“The countries that comprise China’s Shadow Transshipment Network include many of America’s largest trading partners,” the report said.
“China’s biggest enablers range from Mexico and Canada on U.S. land borders to the European Union, India, Japan, and South Korea.”
